title: Fed Still Cautious: Why Victory Over Inflation Remains Out of Reach, Fox Business Reports
body:
The Federal Reserve’s latest policy meeting concluded with a modest 25‑basis‑point hike to the federal funds rate, a move that signals the central bank is not yet prepared to declare a win in its battle against inflation. While the decision was broadly expected, markets are already pricing in the likelihood of one or two additional increases before the calendar turns, underscoring the persistence of price pressures that remain well above the Fed’s 2 percent target.

The rate increase brings the benchmark to the 5.25‑5.50 percent range, the highest level in more than two decades. Yet, the Fed’s own projections suggest that headline consumer‑price inflation could still hover near 3 percent through the summer, with core inflation—excluding food and energy—running even hotter. The central bank’s “dot‑plot” of future policy, released alongside the decision, shows three of the 19 voting members forecasting a total of three hikes by the end of 2024, while the median expectation points to a modest two‑rate‑cut scenario in 2025. In other words, policymakers are bracing for a longer tightening cycle than many investors had hoped.

Economists point to several factors that keep the inflation outlook uneasy. First, wages are beginning to rise at a pace not seen since the early 2000s, feeding into service‑sector costs that are notoriously sticky. Second, supply‑chain disruptions—particularly in semiconductors, freight, and energy—have not fully resolved, leaving price gaps that can quickly translate into broader CPI gains. Finally, the recent rebound in consumer spending, bolstered by a still‑robust labor market, adds demand‑side pressure that could offset any gains from tighter credit conditions.

The reaction in financial markets has been mixed. Treasury yields slipped slightly after the announcement, reflecting a modest easing of expectations for aggressive further hikes, while the dollar weakened against a basket of major currencies as investors recalibrated risk appetites. Equities, especially rate‑sensitive sectors such as technology and real estate, experienced a brief sell‑off before stabilizing, suggesting that investors are digesting the notion of a gradual, data‑driven approach rather than a rapid series of large moves.

Policy makers themselves remain cautious in their public messaging. One Federal Reserve governor, speaking at a recent conference, warned that “inflation is still too high to be complacent” and highlighted the importance of “allowing the economy to absorb the cumulative impact of monetary tightening.” The governor’s remarks echo the Fed’s longstanding “dual mandate” philosophy, which balances price stability with maximum employment, and suggest that any premature declaration of victory could jeopardize both goals.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of inflation will hinge on a handful of key variables. The pace of wage growth, the resolution of lingering supply bottlenecks, and the trajectory of global energy prices will all feed into the Fed’s next policy decision, likely slated for early December. If inflation continues to trend downward toward the 2 percent goal, the central bank may adopt a more dovish stance, potentially pausing or even reversing rate hikes. Conversely, any resurgence of price pressures could compel the Fed to accelerate its tightening timetable, extending the period of higher borrowing costs for businesses and consumers alike.

In sum, the latest rate hike reflects a cautious, incremental approach by the Federal Reserve as it navigates an inflationary environment that remains stubbornly above target. While the path forward is still uncertain, the central bank’s willingness to keep policy flexible suggests that future moves will be dictated by incoming data rather than predetermined timelines. Investors, businesses, and households should therefore prepare for a continued period of monetary tightening, with the ultimate outcome dependent on how quickly the economy can absorb the cumulative impact of higher rates and bring inflation back to the Fed’s long‑standing 2 percent benchmark.
